To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

, in most circumstances of depressed ART financing in low and medium income countries, the most ethical ART eligibility policy is to reserve all ART for sickers, and that this is the case because it is "cross theoreti-cally dominant."

in most circumstances of depressed funding in low and middle countries, it is more ethically justified to reserve all ART for the sicker patients, rather than to make ART available immediately on diagnosis to all patients, regardless of their health status.
, in most circumstances of depressed funding in low and middle-income countries with generalized HIV epidemic, reserving treatment for the sickest is ethically preferable.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to best use limited resources in the context of the AIDS epidemic. We argue that the best way is to prioritize those who are the sickest.
the question of who should be eligible for antiretrovirals (ARVs), in the context of the most important ethical approaches.
the question: when the global budget for HIV/AIDS cannot cover all patients, who should be eligible for ART?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

, in most circumstances of depressed funding in low and middle-income countries with generalized HIV/ AIDS epidemics, the ethical approach that prioritizes saving the most life years, life years, or quality adjusted life years is that of reserving all antiretrovival therapy for sicker patients.

in most circumstances of depressed funding in most low and medium income countries, reserving all antiretrovial therapy (ART) for sicker patients, and not offering ART immediately to all patients, is more ethical than current international standards, which are based on "universal test and trear".
the current ART eligibility standard of "universal test and treatment," is ethically problematic, and should be replaced by a standard that reserves ART for sicker people.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the current international standard for ART eligibility is not ethically defensible in the context of global ART budgets that are insufficient to cover all patients.
, if the global ART budget cannot cover all patients, the most ethical way to prioritize is to give all ART to the sickest patients.
, when budgets cannot cover all patients, the sickest should come first. (C) 2016 Elsevier Ireland Ltd. All rights reserved
The main takeaway from our work is that

the ethical case for universal test and treat in low and middle-income countries is weaker than the case for ART for the sickest patients, and that, in the event of a budget cut, the latter should take precedence over the former.
, in the face of budget cuts, it may not be ethical to prioritize ART on diagnosis, even for those with the highest CD4 count.
, in most circumstances of depressed funding for HIV/AIDS, it is unethical for countries to provide ART for healthier patients immediately after diagnosis.
